messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 70
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Welder
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 80

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Entrapment: Having no options, Violence: Violence, Auditory/Threat: Gunshot noise
  Maladaptive Strategies: Memory Detachment: I detach myself from the memories, Fawn Response: become overly compliant when feeling threatened, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Memory: Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
  Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Vignette:
Rafael had lived most of his adult life in the United States with a working routine that centered on steel, heat, and noise, first in shipyards and later as a welder in a fabrication shop on the edge of town. Now at 70, widowed and living alone, he had finally agreed to talk about what had happened years earlier, though even in the first appointments he kept his gaze on the floor and spoke as if he were measuring each word. The event he described was not easy for him to hold in one piece. In his early thirties, during a period of political violence in Latin America before he came to the United States, he had been taken and held by men who questioned him and beat him, keeping him trapped where there was no way out. He remembered the suffocating sense of being boxed in, with the knowledge that his own movements were controlled by others and that one wrong look or gesture could bring more harm. Gunfire had been part of that world around him, and the sharp crack of gunshot noise still cut through him decades later. When he tried to tell the story, he would begin with one detail, then lose the thread and stop, saying only that he could not explain it properly, as though the experience scattered his mind before the account could be finished.

What stayed with Rafael was not a distant recollection but something he experienced as happening again. When he remembered the torture, he did not speak of it as finished history; his expression changed and he would say that it felt as if he were back there in the same moment, with the same helplessness pressing in on him. He often became intensely angry when the memory surfaced, an anger that seemed to rise suddenly and then leave him ashamed of how strongly it flooded him. Over the years he developed habits meant to keep the memories at bay. He tried hard not to think about the trauma, pushing it away whenever it appeared. When reminders came, he described detaching himself from the memories, as if stepping back from his own mind made the images less immediate. He also noticed that when he felt threatened, especially if another person seemed impatient, controlling, or unpredictable, he became overly compliant. In the welding shop this showed up in very concrete ways: if a supervisor raised his voice or pressed him to hurry, Rafael would nod quickly, agree to extra work, and avoid saying no, even when he was tired. He seemed to believe that being agreeable might keep things calm, that making himself smaller and easier would reduce the chance of danger.

Certain moments in daily life still hit him with unusual force. A sudden gunshot noise, whether from fireworks in the neighborhood or a backfire near the shop, could make his body go rigid before he had time to think. Being stuck with no clear exit mattered to him in a way that others did not always understand. If he found himself in a crowded waiting room, boxed into a chair, or even standing in a narrow aisle at a store when people pressed too close, he became tense and watchful, scanning for a way to move. Those moments carried the same emotional shape as the original captivity: not simply discomfort, but the sense that options had vanished and that something violent could happen before he could protect himself. He came to think that you could never know who would harm you, and that belief colored the way he moved through ordinary situations. It made him wary of strangers, of sudden changes in tone, of any setting where he could not immediately gauge what another person intended.

Rafael’s self-understanding was burdened by guilt that had never really eased. He said he would never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened, even though in the telling it was clear that he had been trapped and outmatched. Still, he returned again and again to the idea that he should have acted differently, should have found a way to resist, should have protected himself or others better. He also blamed himself for the event, as if some way he had behaved had somehow invited the violence that followed. These thoughts sat alongside the fear, and at times they seemed to make his memory of the torture even harder to approach, because remembering meant feeling both the rage of what had been done to him and the reproach he directed inward.

Since his wife’s death, the apartment had become quieter and more empty, and that silence gave the memories more room to intrude. He had kept working as long as he could, but he noticed that the shop’s clang of metal and sharp bursts of noise made him more watchful, especially on days when a sudden bang echoed off the walls. He finally sought help because he was tired of living as if the past were still happening in the present. He wanted to understand why he could not speak clearly about what had been done to him and why he still reacted so strongly to noise, confinement, and the sense of being at someone else’s mercy. More than anything, Rafael said he hoped he might learn how to live without feeling that danger could come from anywhere, and without carrying the belief that he was the one who had failed.
